intro.why: Recurrent models introduced the ideas of state, gating and sequence-level training that underpin attention (Module 8) and Transformers (Module 9), and gated RNNs remain strong for streaming and time-series problems.

sections.title: Motivation: why sequence models?
sections.body: Many real-world problems involve sequential data: natural language ("The cat sat on the ___"), time-series forecasting (stock prices, temperature, sensor data), speech (audio over time), video (frame sequences), genomics (DNA/protein sequences). Key characteristic: order matters, and dependencies exist across time steps (the figure links every earlier word to the blank).

sections.title: Why feed-forward networks fail
sections.plain: Fixed size, no memory, no sharing across positions.
sections.body: Key issues: fixed input size (cannot handle variable-length sequences); no memory (each input processed independently); no parameter sharing (different weights for each position). Example: predict the next word in "I grew up in France, so I speak fluent ___": the model needs context from 7 words back ("France") to predict "French", but a feed-forward network treats each position independently. We need a model that can remember past information.

sections.title: Temporal dependencies
sections.body: Short-term dependencies: the needed information is recent ("The clouds are in the ___" → "sky"). Long-term dependencies: information far back ("I grew up in France… I speak fluent ___" → "French"). Challenge: the model must learn to remember relevant information and forget irrelevant information; different sequence lengths require flexible architectures.

sections.title: Autoregressive models
sections.body:
$$P(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^TP(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})\qquad(1)$$

Autoregressive property: the current value depends on previous values:

$$P(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})=f(x_{t-1},x_{t-2},\dots,x_1)\qquad(2)$$

Challenge: how much history to consider? $t$ grows over time. Equation (1) is exact (chain rule of probability), not an assumption.

sections.title: Autoregressive example
sections.plain: Each word depends on all previous words.
sections.body:
$$P(\text{The, cat, sat, on, the, mat})=P(\text{The})\times P(\text{cat}\mid\text{The})\times P(\text{sat}\mid\text{The, cat})\times P(\text{on}\mid\text{The, cat, sat})\times P(\text{the}\mid\text{The, cat, sat, on})\times P(\text{mat}\mid\text{The, cat, sat, on, the})$$

Each word depends on all previous words; the history grows with sequence length. A full table of conditionals for vocabulary $V$ and history length $t$ would need $V^t$ entries.

sections.title: Markov assumption
sections.plain: Truncate the history to k steps.
sections.body:
$$\text{First order: }P(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})\approx P(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\ (3),\qquad k\text{-th order: }P(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})\approx P(x_t\mid x_{t-k},\dots,x_{t-1})\ (4)$$

Advantage: fixed-size context, tractable computation. Disadvantage: may lose important long-term dependencies. An n-gram language model is an $(n-1)$-th order Markov model with $V^n$ parameters.

sections.title: Markov example: bigram and trigram
sections.plain: P(mat | the) and P(mat | on, the).
sections.body: First-order (bigram): $P(\text{mat}\mid\text{The, cat, sat, on, the})\approx P(\text{mat}\mid\text{the})$. Second-order (trigram): $\approx P(\text{mat}\mid\text{on, the})$. Key insight: a fixed context window (1 or 2 words) ignores earlier words like "cat" and "sat": computationally efficient but limited expressiveness.

sections.title: Latent variable models
sections.plain: Summarise the past in a hidden state h_t.
sections.body:
$$h_t=f(x_t,h_{t-1})\quad(5),\qquad P(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})=P(x_t\mid h_t)\quad(6)$$

Key insight: $h_t$ is a latent (hidden) variable that contains a compressed summary of history, has a fixed-size representation regardless of sequence length, and is updated recursively at each step: the foundation of RNNs. (Strictly, (6) predicts $x_{t+1}$ from $h_t$ in the usual indexing; a commonly quoted version writes it for $x_t$.) Example: $h_0\to h_1$ (The) $\to h_2$ (cat) $\to\dots\to h_5$ (the) → predict "mat": $h_5$ summarises "The cat sat on the"; predict $P(\text{mat}\mid h_5)$; $h_t$ is fixed-size regardless of length.

sections.title: Latent state intuition
sections.body: The hidden state is a learned, lossy compression: unlike a Markov window it can, in principle, retain "cat" (subject) while forgetting filler words. Whether it actually does depends on training, which is where vanishing gradients and gating come in.

sections.title: Numerical example: temperature forecasting (AR)
sections.body: Task: predict tomorrow's temperature (regression) from 20, 22, 25, 24, 21 °C. Approach 1, first-order autoregressive: $T_{t+1}=\alpha T_t+\beta$ with $\alpha=0.8$, $\beta=4.0$ learned from history. If today is 25 °C: $T_{tomorrow}=0.8\times25+4.0=24.0$ °C. Prediction: $T_5=21$ → $T_6=0.8\times21+4.0=20.8$ °C; multi-step using the prediction: $T_7=0.8\times20.8+4.0=20.64$ °C. Limitations: only uses the immediate past; cannot capture weekly/seasonal patterns; errors accumulate in multi-step predictions (and the forecasts converge to the fixed point $\beta/(1-\alpha)=20$ °C).

sections.title: Temperature forecasting: latent variable model
sections.body: Approach 2: a hidden state $h_t\in\mathbb R^d$ captures the weather pattern/trend (warming, cooling, stable; seasonal effects): $\hat T_{t+1}=g(h_t)$, $h_t=f(T_t,h_{t-1})$. Over 20, 22, 25, 24, 21: $h_1$ captures the starting point; $h_2$ a warming trend (20 → 22); $h_3$ strong warming (20 → 22 → 25); $h_4$ peak reached at 25 °C, cooling starts; $h_5$ cooling continues (25 → 24 → 21): it encodes the trajectory, not just the last value. The prediction uses full context: $\hat T_6=g(h_5)$ might predict 19–20 °C (continued cooling).

sections.title: Comparing the two approaches
sections.plain: AR uses one value; RNN uses a summary.
sections.body: The AR(1) model predicts 20.8 °C because it only sees today's 21 °C and pulls towards its fixed point (20 °C). A state that remembers the trend predicts lower because the last two days fell. The interactive lab uses a hand-made trend state $h_t=a\,h_{t-1}+(1-a)(T_t-T_{t-1})$ with forecast $T_t+h_t$: with $a=0.5$, $h_5=-1.25$ and $\hat T_6=19.75$ °C. A trained RNN learns its own $f$ and $g$ from data instead.

sections.title: Recurrent neural network
sections.plain: A network with a loop; same parameters every step.
sections.body: Definition: a neural network with loops, allowing information to persist. Key ideas: process sequential data one step at a time; maintain a hidden state that summarises past information; share the same parameters across all time steps. The loop: $h_t$ feeds back into the cell at the next step ($x_t$ → RNN → $o_t$, with the recurrent connection $h_t$).

sections.title: Unrolled computation graph
sections.plain: One copy per time step, same W_hx, W_hh, W_ho.
sections.body: Unrolling visualises the RNN across time steps: $x_1\to h_1\to o_1$, $x_2\to h_2\to o_2$, …, with $h_1\to h_2\to h_3\to h_4\to\cdots$. Every vertical edge uses the same $W_{hx}$ (input) and $W_{ho}$ (output), every horizontal edge the same $W_{hh}$. Unrolled, the RNN is a deep feed-forward network with tied weights, which is how it is trained.

sections.title: Mathematical formulation I: hidden state
sections.plain: h_t = φ(W_hh h_{t−1} + W_hx x_t + b_h).
sections.body:
$$h_t=\phi(W_{hh}h_{t-1}+W_{hx}x_t+b_h)\qquad(7)$$

$x_t\in\mathbb R^d$ input; $h_t\in\mathbb R^h$ hidden state; $W_{hx}\in\mathbb R^{h\times d}$ input-to-hidden; $W_{hh}\in\mathbb R^{h\times h}$ hidden-to-hidden (recurrent); $b_h\in\mathbb R^h$; $\phi$ typically tanh or ReLU. Initial state $h_0=\mathbf 0$ or a learned parameter.

sections.title: Mathematical formulation II: output
sections.body:
$$o_t=W_{ho}h_t+b_o\quad(8),\qquad P(x_t=k\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})=\frac{\exp(o_t^{(k)})}{\sum_{j=1}^V\exp(o_t^{(j)})}\quad(9)$$

$o_t\in\mathbb R^V$ output logits; $W_{ho}\in\mathbb R^{V\times h}$; $b_o\in\mathbb R^V$; $V$ vocabulary size for language modelling. (As in (6), the logits computed at step $t$ are used to predict the next token.)

sections.title: Parameter sharing across time
sections.plain: Fixed parameter count for any length.
sections.body: The same parameters are used at every step: $W_{hx},W_{hh},b_h$ and $W_{ho},b_o$ are shared across all time steps. Advantages: (1) a fixed number of parameters regardless of sequence length; (2) sequences of any length can be processed; (3) generalisation: patterns learned at one position transfer to others. Contrast: a feed-forward network uses different weights for each position.

sections.title: RNN parameter counting
sections.plain: hd + h² + h + Vh + V = h(d + h + V + 1) + V.
sections.body: $$W_{hx}:h\times d,\quad W_{hh}:h\times h,\quad b_h:h,\quad W_{ho}:V\times h,\quad b_o:V;\qquad \text{Total}=hd+h^2+h+Vh+V=h(d+h+V+1)+V\ \ $$

sections.title: Parameter counting example
sections.body: $W_{hx}:256\times100=25{,}600$; $W_{hh}:256\times256=65{,}536$; $b_h:256$; $W_{ho}:10{,}000\times256=2{,}560{,}000$; $b_o:10{,}000$. Total 2,661,392 parameters, verified; 96% are in the output layer, which is why large-vocabulary models use tied embeddings or sampled softmax.

sections.title: Activation functions in RNNs
sections.body: tanh: range [−1, 1], centred at zero (helps gradient flow), most common for vanilla RNNs. ReLU: range [0, ∞), can help with vanishing gradients but may cause exploding activations because $h_t$ can grow without bound through repeated multiplication by $W_{hh}$ (IRNN uses ReLU with identity initialisation and careful scaling).

sections.title: Training objective
sections.body:
Learn $\theta=\{W_{hx},W_{hh},W_{ho},b_h,b_o\}$ to maximise sequence likelihood over $N$ training sequences:

$$\theta^*=\arg\max_\theta\prod_{i=1}^NP(x_1^{(i)},\dots,x_T^{(i)}\mid\theta)\ (10),\qquad \theta^*=\arg\max_\theta\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T\log P(x_t^{(i)}\mid x_1^{(i)},\dots,x_{t-1}^{(i)},\theta)\ (11)$$$$\mathcal L(\theta)=-\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^T\log P(x_t^{(i)}\mid x_1^{(i)},\dots,x_{t-1}^{(i)},\theta)\qquad(12)$$

sections.title: Loss function for sequences
sections.body:
$$\ell_t=-\sum_{k=1}^V\mathbb 1[x_t=k]\log P(x_t=k\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})\ (13),\quad \mathcal L=\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t=-\sum_{t=1}^T\log P(x_t\mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1})\ (14),\quad \bar{\mathcal L}=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t\ (15)$$

The average per-token loss is typically reported during training; $\exp(\bar{\mathcal L})$ is the perplexity, the effective number of equally likely next tokens.

sections.title: Backpropagation through time
sections.plain: Unroll, backprop from T to 1, sum gradients.
sections.body: Challenge: parameters are shared across all steps, the hidden state depends on the entire history, so we must backpropagate through time. Key insight: unroll the RNN into a feed-forward network, apply standard backpropagation, and sum gradients from all steps (parameter sharing). BPTT: forward pass computes outputs for all steps; backward pass computes gradients from $t=T$ to $t=1$. Truncated BPTT backpropagates only $k$ steps to bound cost and memory.

sections.title: BPTT computational graph
sections.plain: Gradients accumulate contributions from future steps.
sections.body: Forward (orange): $x_t\to h_t\to o_t\to\ell_t$ for each step; backward (red dashed): gradients flow from $\ell_t$ down to $h_t$ and from $h_{t+1}$ back to $h_t$. Gradients accumulate contributions from all future time steps.

sections.title: BPTT key gradient equations
sections.body:
$$\mathcal L=\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t\ (16),\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial o_t}=\frac{\partial\ell_t}{\partial o_t}\ (17),\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_t}=\frac{\partial\ell_t}{\partial h_t}+\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_{t+1}}\frac{\partial h_{t+1}}{\partial h_t}\ (18),\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W}=\sum_{t=1}^T\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_t}\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial W}\ (19)$$

With $h_{t+1}=\tanh(W_{hh}h_t+W_{hx}x_{t+1})$: $\frac{\partial h_{t+1}}{\partial h_t}=\text{diag}(1-h_{t+1}^2)W_{hh}$, and in (19) $\partial h_t/\partial W$ means the local (immediate) dependence at step $t$.

sections.title: BPTT numerical example: setup
sections.plain: d = h = V = 2; no biases; tanh.
sections.body: 3 time steps: $W_{hh}=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.3\\0.2&0.4\end{bmatrix}$, $W_{hx}=\begin{bmatrix}0.4&0.3\\0.2&0.5\end{bmatrix}$, $W_{ho}=\begin{bmatrix}0.6&0.4\\0.3&0.7\end{bmatrix}$, $b_h=b_o=\mathbf 0$, $\phi=\tanh$; inputs $x_1=[1,0]^T$, $x_2=[0,1]^T$, $x_3=[1,1]^T$; $h_0=\mathbf 0$.

sections.title: BPTT: backward pass
sections.body: Targets $y_1=[1,0]^T$, $y_2=[0,1]^T$, $y_3=[1,0]^T$; softmax probabilities from $o_t$. Output gradient (softmax + cross-entropy): $\frac{\partial\ell_3}{\partial o_3}=\text{softmax}(o_3)-y_3=[-0.496,0.496]^T$ (ours −0.497). Hidden gradient at $t=3$: $\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_3}=W_{ho}^T\frac{\partial\ell_3}{\partial o_3}=[-0.149,0.149]^T$. At $t=2$ (recursive): $\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_2}=\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial h_2}+\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_3}\frac{\partial h_3}{\partial h_2}$ with $\frac{\partial h_3}{\partial h_2}=\text{diag}(1-h_3^2)\cdot W_{hh}$. Numerically (with correct forward values): $\partial\mathcal L/\partial h_2=[0.134,-0.140]$, $\partial\mathcal L/\partial h_1=[-0.114,0.139]$.

sections.title: BPTT: parameter gradients
sections.plain: Sums over time of local gradients.
sections.body:
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W_{ho}}=\sum_{t=1}^3\frac{\partial\ell_t}{\partial o_t}h_t^T\ (20),\quad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W_{hh}}=\sum_{t=1}^3\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_t}\cdot\text{diag}(1-h_t^2)\cdot h_{t-1}^T\ (21),\quad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W_{hx}}=\sum_{t=1}^3\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_t}\cdot\text{diag}(1-h_t^2)\cdot x_t^T\ (22)$$

All parameter gradients are sums over time steps; then gradient descent $W\leftarrow W-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W}$. Results (code ex1): $\partial\mathcal L/\partial W_{ho}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.340&-0.197\\0.340&0.197\end{bmatrix}$, $\partial\mathcal L/\partial W_{hh}=\begin{bmatrix}0.012&-0.010\\-0.006&0.016\end{bmatrix}$, $\partial\mathcal L/\partial W_{hx}=\begin{bmatrix}-0.149&0.049\\0.193&-0.034\end{bmatrix}$.

sections.title: Vanishing gradients: the problem
sections.body:
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_t}=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_{t+1}}\frac{\partial h_{t+1}}{\partial h_t}=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_{t+1}}\cdot\text{diag}(\phi'(z_t))\cdot W_{hh}\ (23),\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_1}=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial h_T}\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}\text{diag}(\phi'(z_t))\cdot W_{hh}\ (24)$$

A product of many matrices: if $\|W_{hh}\|<1$ and $|\phi'|<1$ (tanh), the gradient vanishes; if $\|W_{hh}\|>1$, it can explode. Consequences: long-term dependencies are hard to learn; early steps receive negligible gradient signal. (Strictly, the bound uses $\|W_{hh}\|\cdot\max|\phi'|$: tanh′ ≤ 1 so a large spectral norm is necessary but not sufficient for explosion.)

sections.title: Vanishing gradients: numerical example
sections.body:
Setup: $h=3$, $W_{hh}$ with $\lambda_{max}=0.8$, $|\phi'(z_t)|\approx0.5$. Gradient ratio across $k$ steps:

$$k=5:\ (0.8\times0.5)^5=0.4^5=0.01024;\qquad k=10:\ 0.4^{10}=0.0001;\qquad k=20:\ 0.4^{20}\approx10^{-8}.$$

The gradient at $t=1$ is $10^{-8}$ times the gradient at $t=20$: early steps get almost no learning signal; long-term dependencies cannot be learned.

sections.title: Why vanishing gradients are problematic
sections.body: Learning difficulty: parameters affecting early time steps barely update; the model cannot learn long-term patterns; training becomes ineffective for long sequences. Failure scenarios: "I grew up in France… [50 words]… I speak fluent ___"; long-range syntactic dependencies; time series with seasonal (yearly) patterns. Solutions: better architectures (LSTM, GRU), careful initialisation (orthogonal $W_{hh}$), skip connections. For exploding gradients: gradient clipping, $g\leftarrow g\cdot\min(1,\tau/\|g\|)$.

sections.title: Bidirectional RNNs: motivation
sections.body: Standard RNNs only use past context, predicting from $x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}$. Many tasks benefit from full context: sentiment ("The movie was not ___": need "good" or "bad"); named entity recognition ("I met Paris in Paris": person vs city); speech recognition (future phonemes disambiguate the current sound); machine translation. Key idea: a forward RNN left-to-right, a backward RNN right-to-left, combine both.

sections.title: Bidirectional architecture
sections.body: Each input $x_t$ feeds a forward state $\overrightarrow h_t$ (chain $x_1\to x_T$) and a backward state $\overleftarrow h_t$ (chain $x_T\to x_1$); each output $o_t$ uses both.

sections.title: Bidirectional formulation
sections.body:
$$\overrightarrow h_t=\phi(W_{\overrightarrow{hh}}\overrightarrow h_{t-1}+W_{\overrightarrow{hx}}x_t+b_{\overrightarrow h})\ (25),\qquad \overleftarrow h_t=\phi(W_{\overleftarrow{hh}}\overleftarrow h_{t+1}+W_{\overleftarrow{hx}}x_t+b_{\overleftarrow h})\ (26)$$$$h_t=[\overrightarrow h_t;\overleftarrow h_t]\ (27),\qquad o_t=W_{ho}h_t+b_o=W_{ho}[\overrightarrow h_t;\overleftarrow h_t]+b_o\ (28)$$

$[\,;\,]$ denotes concatenation.

sections.title: Bidirectional parameter counting
sections.plain: h_f² + h_b² + d(h_f + h_b) + V(h_f + h_b) + h_f + h_b + V.
sections.body:
Forward: $W_{\overrightarrow{hx}}:h_f\times d$, $W_{\overrightarrow{hh}}:h_f\times h_f$, $b:h_f$; backward: $h_b\times d$, $h_b\times h_b$, $h_b$; output $W_{ho}:V\times(h_f+h_b)$, $b_o:V$:

$$\text{Total}=h_f^2+h_b^2+d(h_f+h_b)+V(h_f+h_b)+h_f+h_b+V.$$

Example: $d=100$, $h_f=h_b=128$, $V=10{,}000$: forward $12{,}800+16{,}384+128=29{,}312$; backward 29,312; output $10{,}000\times256=2{,}560{,}000$ plus 10,000; total $29{,}312+29{,}312+2{,}570{,}000=2{,}628{,}624$ (verified).

sections.title: When to use bidirectional RNNs
sections.plain: Whole sequence available; not for real-time/causal.
sections.body: Use when: the entire sequence is available before prediction and the task benefits from future context (text classification, NER, translation encoders). Do not use when: real-time/online prediction is required; causal modelling (future cannot influence past): language modelling, real-time speech recognition, time-series forecasting. Key limitation: must process the entire sequence first; higher computational cost (two RNNs); not suitable for streaming.

sections.title: Deep (stacked) RNNs: motivation
sections.body: Why stack: a single RNN layer has limited capacity; deep networks learn hierarchical features: lower layers simple patterns, higher layers complex abstract ones. Examples: text characters → words → phrases → sentences; speech phonemes → syllables → words; time series short-term → medium-term → long-term trends. Empirically, deeper RNNs often beat wider single-layer RNNs; typical depth 2–4 layers (diminishing returns beyond).

sections.title: Deep RNN architecture
sections.body: Each layer processes the output of the previous layer: horizontal arrows are recurrent connections within a layer, vertical arrows feed-forward connections between layers (three layers $h^{(1)},h^{(2)},h^{(3)}$ over three steps).

sections.title: Deep RNN formulation
sections.body:
$$h_t^{(\ell)}=\phi\big(W_{hh}^{(\ell)}h_{t-1}^{(\ell)}+W_{hx}^{(\ell)}h_t^{(\ell-1)}+b_h^{(\ell)}\big)\quad(29),\qquad o_t=W_{ho}h_t^{(L)}+b_o\quad(30)$$

$h_t^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{h_\ell}$; $W_{hh}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{h_\ell\times h_\ell}$; $W_{hx}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb R^{h_\ell\times h_{\ell-1}}$; $h_t^{(0)}=x_t$. Each layer learns a different level of abstraction.

sections.title: Deep RNN parameter counting
sections.plain: h₁d + Σ(h_ℓ² + h_ℓ) + Σ h_ℓh_{ℓ−1} + Vh_L + V.
sections.body:
Layer 1: $W_{hx}^{(1)}:h_1\times d$, $W_{hh}^{(1)}:h_1\times h_1$, $b^{(1)}:h_1$ → $h_1d+h_1^2+h_1$. Layer $\ell\ge2$: $h_\ell h_{\ell-1}+h_\ell^2+h_\ell$. Output: $Vh_L+V$:

$$\text{Total}=h_1d+\sum_{\ell=1}^L(h_\ell^2+h_\ell)+\sum_{\ell=2}^Lh_\ell h_{\ell-1}+Vh_L+V.$$

sections.title: Deep RNN worked example
sections.plain: 2 layers; t = 1 exact; t = 2 reference values off.

sections.title: Deep RNN gradient flow
sections.plain: Vanishing through time and depth; 2–4 layers.
sections.body: Gradients must flow through time (horizontal) and depth (vertical): a compound vanishing-gradient problem, more severe than in a single-layer RNN. Mitigation: LSTM/GRU cells, residual connections between layers, careful initialisation, layer normalisation. Practical limit: typically 2–4 layers; deeper networks are harder to train with diminishing returns beyond 4.

sections.title: GRU: motivation
sections.body: Vanilla RNN problems: vanishing gradients prevent learning long-term dependencies; all information in the hidden state is weighted equally; no mechanism to selectively remember or forget. Key insight: gates, neural layers with sigmoid activation $\sigma\in[0,1]$, control information flow ($\sigma=0$ blocks, $\sigma=1$ passes, in between partially). GRU advantages: learns what to remember and forget; better gradient flow; captures long-term dependencies; fewer parameters than LSTM (Cho et al., 2014).

sections.title: GRU architecture
sections.plain: Reset r, update z, candidate h̃, interpolation.
sections.body: Two gates: the reset gate $r_t$ controls how much past information to forget; the update gate $z_t$ controls how much to update the hidden state. A candidate $\tilde h_t$ proposes new content; the final $h_t$ interpolates between old and new; all gates are learned. Unrolled: each GRU cell contains $r_t,z_t,\tilde h_t$; the hidden state flows through time; the same GRU parameters are shared across steps.

sections.title: GRU reset gate
sections.plain: r_t = σ(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t−1} + b_r).
sections.body:
$$r_t=\sigma(W_rx_t+U_rh_{t-1}+b_r)\qquad(31)$$

Decides how much past information to forget: $r_t\approx0$ ignores the previous hidden state (reset memory); $r_t\approx1$ keeps it; element-wise, so different dimensions reset differently. Intuition: when a new topic starts, the reset gate can forget irrelevant past.

sections.title: GRU update gate
sections.plain: z_t = σ(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t−1} + b_z).
sections.body:
$$z_t=\sigma(W_zx_t+U_zh_{t-1}+b_z)\qquad(32)$$

Decides how much to update the hidden state, acting like a "memory gate". With equation (34): $z_t\approx1$ keeps the old state, $z_t\approx0$ replaces it with the candidate. A commonly quoted version says "$z_t\approx0$: keep old state; $z_t\approx1$: replace with new candidate" and "keep $z_t$ small to preserve information", which is the opposite of (34) (it matches the alternative convention $h_t=(1-z_t)h_{t-1}+z_t\tilde h_t$ used in some texts). Under the stated (34) and (35), long-term memory needs $z_t$ large, as the convention above requires.

sections.title: GRU candidate hidden state
sections.plain: h̃_t = tanh(W_h x_t + U_h(r_t ⊙ h_{t−1}) + b_h).
sections.body:
$$\tilde h_t=\tanh\big(W_hx_t+U_h(r_t\odot h_{t-1})+b_h\big)\qquad(33)$$

Computes new candidate content: like the vanilla RNN update, but the past is first scaled by the reset gate; $r_t\approx0$ computes from $x_t$ only, $r_t\approx1$ uses the full past; tanh gives range [−1, 1].

sections.title: GRU final hidden state; computational graph
sections.body:
$$h_t=z_t\odot h_{t-1}+(1-z_t)\odot\tilde h_t\qquad(34)$$

Linear interpolation: $z_t=0$: $h_t=\tilde h_t$ (new candidate); $z_t=1$: $h_t=h_{t-1}$ (keep old); $z_t=0.5$: a 50/50 blend. The update gate controls how much information flows from the past, which helps gradient flow. Graph: $h_{t-1}$ and $x_t$ feed reset (σ), update (σ) and candidate (tanh) blocks; $r_t\odot h_{t-1}$ feeds the candidate; $z_t$, $(1-z_t)$ and $\tilde h_t$ combine by multiplication and addition into $h_t$.

sections.title: GRU numerical example
sections.body:
Setup: $d=h=2$; $W_r=\begin{bmatrix}0.3&0.2\\0.1&0.4\end{bmatrix}$, $U_r=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.1\\0.2&0.3\end{bmatrix}$, $W_z=\begin{bmatrix}0.4&0.3\\0.2&0.5\end{bmatrix}$, $U_z=\begin{bmatrix}0.3&0.2\\0.1&0.4\end{bmatrix}$, $W_h=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.3\\0.2&0.4\end{bmatrix}$, $U_h=\begin{bmatrix}0.4&0.2\\0.1&0.3\end{bmatrix}$, all biases 0; $x_t=[1.0,0.5]^T$, $h_{t-1}=[0.6,0.4]^T$.

Step 1: $r_t=\sigma([0.4,0.3]+[0.34,0.24])=\sigma([0.74,0.54])=[0.677,0.632]$. Step 2: $z_t=\sigma([0.55,0.45]+[0.26,0.22])=\sigma([0.81,0.67])=[0.692,0.662]$. Step 3: $r_t\odot h_{t-1}=[0.406,0.253]$. Step 4: $\tilde h_t=\tanh([0.65,0.40]+[0.213,0.116])=[0.696,0.475]$ (ours 0.698). Step 5: $h_t=[0.692,0.662]\odot[0.6,0.4]+[0.308,0.338]\odot[0.696,0.475]=[0.415,0.265]+[0.214,0.161]=[0.629,0.426]$ (recomputed without intermediate rounding: $[0.630,0.425]$). Interpretation: $z_t\approx[0.69,0.66]$ mostly keeps the old state; $r_t\approx[0.68,0.63]$ uses most of the past for the candidate; the final state is ≈ 69% old, 31% new (verified, code ex2).

sections.title: GRU parameter counting; why it helps gradients
sections.body:
Parameters: reset, update and candidate each have $W:h\times d$, $U:h\times h$, $b:h$; output $W_{ho}:V\times h$, $b_o:V$: total $3hd+3h^2+3h+Vh+V$. For $d=100$, $h=256$: $3(256\cdot100+256^2+256)+256V+V=274{,}176+257V$.

$$\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}=z_t+(1-z_t)\odot\frac{\partial\tilde h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}\qquad(35)$$

(treating $z_t$ as constant; the full derivative adds terms through $z_t$'s dependence on $h_{t-1}$.) Direct path: $z_t$ connects $h_{t-1}$ to $h_t$ with no weight matrix and no activation derivative; gradients flow directly when $z_t$ is large. Vanilla RNN: $\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}=\text{diag}(\phi'(z_t))\cdot W_{hh}$; GRU adds a term that bypasses the non-linearity, like residual connections in deep networks. For long-term dependencies keep $z_t$ large.

sections.title: LSTM: motivation
sections.plain: Separate cell state (long-term) from hidden state.
sections.body: GRU limitations: one hidden state combines long- and short-term information; the update gate controls both memory and output; less explicit control. LSTM innovation (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997): separate memory from hidden state: cell state $c_t$ (long-term memory, an information highway) and hidden state $h_t$ (short-term working memory), with 3 gates instead of 2. Advantages: uninterrupted gradient flow through the cell; the forget gate selectively removes information; the output gate separates what to remember from what to output; better for very long sequences (100+ steps). The most widely used RNN variant in practice.

sections.title: LSTM architecture
sections.plain: Three gates, two states, candidate c̃_t.
sections.body: Three gates: forget $f_t$ (what to remove from the cell state), input $i_t$ (what new information to add), output $o_t$ (what to output from the cell state). Two states: $c_t$ long-term memory, $h_t$ short-term output; candidate $\tilde c_t$: new information to add. Unrolled: $c_0,h_0$ enter the first cell; the cell state is the upper highway and the hidden state the lower path; both flow through time with shared parameters.

sections.title: LSTM forget gate
sections.plain: f_t = σ(W_f x_t + U_f h_{t−1} + b_f).
sections.body:
$$f_t=\sigma(W_fx_t+U_fh_{t-1}+b_f)\ (36),\qquad c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+\dots\ (37)$$

Decides what to remove from the cell state: $f_t\approx0$ forgets everything; $f_t\approx1$ remembers everything; element-wise. Example: when the topic changes, the forget gate removes old context. Practical tip: initialise $b_f$ around 1 so the LSTM starts by remembering.

sections.title: LSTM input gate and candidate
sections.body:
$$i_t=\sigma(W_ix_t+U_ih_{t-1}+b_i)\ (38),\qquad \tilde c_t=\tanh(W_cx_t+U_ch_{t-1}+b_c)\ (39)$$

$\tilde c_t$ proposes new information; $i_t$ decides how much of it to add ($i_t\approx0$ ignore, $\approx1$ fully accept); together $i_t\odot\tilde c_t$ is added to the cell state.

sections.title: LSTM cell-state update
sections.plain: c_t = f ⊙ c_{t−1} + i ⊙ c̃_t: additive.
sections.body:
$$c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde c_t\qquad(40)$$

Two operations: $f_t\odot c_{t-1}$ forgets selected parts of old memory; $i_t\odot\tilde c_t$ adds selected new information. Key insight: an additive update gives a direct path from $c_{t-1}$ to $c_t$ (when $f_t\approx1$); gradients flow easily through addition with no multiplication by a weight matrix: this is why LSTMs mitigate vanishing gradients.

sections.title: LSTM output gate and hidden state
sections.body:
$$o_t=\sigma(W_ox_t+U_oh_{t-1}+b_o)\ (41),\qquad h_t=o_t\odot\tanh(c_t)\ (42)$$

$\tanh(c_t)$ squashes the cell state to [−1, 1]; $o_t$ decides what parts of the cell state to output, separating what to remember ($c_t$) from what to show ($h_t$): the LSTM can remember without outputting. Graph: forget, input, candidate and output blocks from $h_{t-1}$ and $x_t$; $c_{t-1}\odot f_t$ plus $i_t\odot\tilde c_t$ gives $c_t$; $\tanh(c_t)\odot o_t$ gives $h_t$.

sections.title: LSTM parameter counting; why it solves vanishing gradients
sections.body:
Parameters: forget, input, output gates and candidate each have $W:h\times d$, $U:h\times h$, $b:h$; output layer $V\times h$ and $V$: total $4hd+4h^2+4h+Vh+V$. For $d=100$, $h=256$: $4(256\cdot100+256^2+256)+256V+V=365{,}568+257V$ (verified).

$$\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}}=f_t+(\text{other terms})\qquad(43)$$

Direct additive path: $c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\tilde c_t$ gives $\partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1}=f_t$ (when gates are treated as fixed): no weight-matrix multiplication, no activation derivative; gradients flow uninterrupted when the forget gate is open. The network learns when to open/close gates: for long-term dependencies keep $f_t$ large and $i_t$ small, preserving both information and gradients (the "constant error carousel").

sections.title: LSTM vs GRU
sections.body:
PropertyGRULSTM
Gates2 (reset, update)3 (forget, input, output)
Memory types1 (hidden)2 (cell + hidden)
Parameters$3(hd+h^2+h)$$4(hd+h^2+h)$
Relative paramsFewer (~25% less)More
Training speedFasterSlower
Memory usageLowerHigher
Gradient flowGoodExcellent
Long sequencesGood (50–100 steps)Better (100+ steps)
PopularityIncreasingMost widely used

Use GRU for smaller datasets, shorter sequences, faster training; LSTM for longer sequences, more data, maximum performance. Empirically the two often perform similarly; tune both.

sections.title: Time-series forecasting with RNNs
sections.body:
$$\hat x_{t+1},\hat x_{t+2},\dots,\hat x_{t+k}=f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_t)\qquad(44)$$

Applications: finance (stock prices, portfolio optimisation), weather (temperature, rainfall, wind), energy (electricity demand, solar generation), healthcare (vital signs, disease progression), IoT (sensor prediction, anomaly detection). Why RNNs: capture temporal dependencies automatically, handle variable-length sequences, learn non-linear patterns; LSTM/GRU handle long-term trends and seasonality.

sections.title: Univariate vs multivariate
sections.body: Univariate: a single variable, $x_t\in\mathbb R$ (daily temperature, stock closing price, heart rate). Multivariate: $\mathbf x_t=[x_t^{(1)},\dots,x_t^{(d)}]^T\in\mathbb R^d$ (weather: temp, humidity, pressure; stock: price, volume, volatility; health: heart rate, BP, temperature). Multivariate captures cross-variable dependencies, e.g. humidity affects temperature prediction.

sections.title: Forecasting output types
sections.body: Single-step (many-to-one): predict only the next step, $\hat x_{t+1}\in\mathbb R$; the most common approach. Multi-step (many-to-many): output $[\hat x_{t+1},\dots,\hat x_{t+k}]$ by direct prediction. Alternatives: recursive (feed predictions back, errors accumulate) and sequence-to-sequence encoder–decoders.

sections.title: Complete forecasting example
sections.body:
Problem: predict next day's temperature from a 7-day history with weather features. Input: $\mathbf x_t=[\text{temp},\text{humidity},\text{pressure}]^T\in\mathbb R^3$, sequence $\mathbf x_1..\mathbf x_7$. Model: LSTM with $h=64$: $h_t=\text{LSTM}(\mathbf x_t,h_{t-1},c_{t-1})$, $\hat y_{t+1}=W_oh_7+b_o$ (temperature only). Output $\hat y_{t+1}\in\mathbb R$; multivariate input → univariate output (many-to-one); loss MSE:

$$\mathcal L=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\qquad(45)$$

Parameters: $4(64\cdot3+64^2+64)+65=17{,}473$. Use chronological train/validation/test splits and scale features with training statistics.

sections.title: Evaluation metrics for time series
sections.body: MSE $=\frac1N\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$: penalises large errors heavily; units of the squared target. RMSE $=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}$: same units as the target, more interpretable. MAE $=\frac1N\sum|y_i-\hat y_i|$: less sensitive to outliers, easy to interpret as the average error. Compare against a naïve baseline ("tomorrow = today") and seasonal naïve.

sections.title: Architecture comparison and summary
sections.plain: Vanilla vs GRU vs LSTM; key takeaways.
sections.body:
PropertyVanilla RNNGRULSTM
Gates02 (reset, update)3 (forget, input, output)
Memory states1 (hidden)1 (hidden)2 (cell + hidden)
Activationtanh/ReLUtanh + sigmoidtanh + sigmoid
Parameters (recurrent, with output terms)$2h^2+2hd+2h+Vh$$3h^2+3hd+3h$$4h^2+4hd+4h$
Relative sizeSmallestMedium (~33% less than LSTM's extra)Largest
Gradient flowPoor (vanishing)GoodExcellent
Long sequencesFails (10–20 steps)Good (50–100)Best (100+)
Training speed / memoryFastest / lowestFast / mediumSlower / highest
When to useShort sequences, small modelsGeneral purpose, resource constraintsLong sequences, maximum performance
PopularityRare (baseline)IncreasingMost widely used

(A commonly quoted vanilla-RNN count, $2h^2+2hd+2h+Vh$, is inconsistent with the count derived earlier, $h^2+hd+h+Vh+V$.) Takeaways: recurrent connections process sequences of arbitrary length with shared parameters and a hidden state summarising the past; vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing/exploding gradients; gating (GRU, LSTM) provides controlled information flow, learning what to remember, forget and output; variants: bidirectional (past + future), deep/stacked (hierarchical features), encoder–decoder (variable-length input to variable-length output); applications: time-series forecasting (stocks, weather, energy) and natural language (translation, text generation).

sections.title: Further comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
RNN/LSTM1-D CNN / TCNTransformer
Path length between distant steps$O(T)$$O(\log T)$ (dilated)$O(1)$
Parallel over time (training)NoYesYes
Memory at inference$O(h)$ statereceptive field$O(T)$ KV cache
StreamingNaturalNatural (causal)Needs caching
  • "LSTMs completely solve vanishing gradients." They mitigate them; very long dependencies (1000s of steps) remain hard, which attention addresses.
  • "Teacher forcing is how RNNs predict." It's a training trick (feed true previous tokens); at inference the model feeds its own predictions (exposure bias).
  • "Bigger hidden size fixes long-range memory." Capacity helps, but gradient flow is the bottleneck.

code.title: Vanilla RNN forward pass, BPTT and parameter counts
code.explain: Reproduces the 3-unit forward pass, all parameter counts (RNN, BiRNN, GRU, LSTM), the full 3-step BPTT example with parameter gradients, and the vanishing-gradient arithmetic.
mistakes: Forgetting that W_hh's gradient sums contributions from every time step.
code.notes: In PyTorch, nn.RNN / nn.GRU / nn.LSTM implement these cells; call loss.backward() for BPTT.
code.code:
# Vanilla RNN: the session's forward pass, parameter counts, a full 3-step BPTT example and vanishing-gradient arithmetic
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

# --- Forward pass: d=2, h=3, V=2, tanh ---
Whx = np.array([[0.5, 0.3], [0.2, 0.4], [0.1, 0.2]]); Whh = np.array([[0.3, 0.2, 0.1], [0.1, 0.4, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1, 0.3]])
bh = np.full(3, 0.1); Who = np.array([[0.4, 0.3, 0.5], [0.2, 0.6, 0.1]]); bo = np.full(2, 0.1)
h = np.zeros(3)
for t, x in enumerate([np.array([1.0, 0.5]), np.array([0.8, 1.2])], 1):
    z = Whh @ h + Whx @ x + bh; h = np.tanh(z); o = Who @ h + bo
    print(f"t={t}: z = {z}  h = {h}  o = {o}")

# --- Parameter counts ---
d, hd, V = 100, 256, 10_000
print("vanilla RNN:", hd*d + hd*hd + hd + V*hd + V, "= h(d+h+V+1)+V =", hd*(d + hd + V + 1) + V)
hf = hb = 128
print("bidirectional:", (hf*d + hf*hf + hf) + (hb*d + hb*hb + hb) + V*(hf + hb) + V)
print("GRU recurrent part:", 3*(hd*d + hd*hd + hd), "+ 257V;  LSTM recurrent part:", 4*(hd*d + hd*hd + hd), "+ 257V")
print("LSTM forecaster (d=3, h=64, 1 output):", 4*(64*3 + 64*64 + 64) + 64 + 1)

# --- BPTT example: d=h=V=2, no biases, softmax + cross-entropy ---
Whh = np.array([[0.5, 0.3], [0.2, 0.4]]); Whx = np.array([[0.4, 0.3], [0.2, 0.5]]); Who = np.array([[0.6, 0.4], [0.3, 0.7]])
X = [np.array([1., 0.]), np.array([0., 1.]), np.array([1., 1.])]; Y = [np.array([1., 0.]), np.array([0., 1.]), np.array([1., 0.])]
sm = lambda o: np.exp(o) / np.exp(o).sum()
H = [np.zeros(2)]; O = []
for x in X: H.append(np.tanh(Whh @ H[-1] + Whx @ x)); O.append(Who @ H[-1])
for t in range(3): print(f"BPTT forward t={t+1}: h = {H[t+1]}  o = {O[t]}  p = {sm(O[t])}")
loss = -sum(np.log(sm(O[t]) @ Y[t]) for t in range(3)); print(f"total loss = {loss:.4f}")
dWho = np.zeros_like(Who); dWhh = np.zeros_like(Whh); dWhx = np.zeros_like(Whx); dh_next = np.zeros(2)
for t in reversed(range(3)):
    do = sm(O[t]) - Y[t]; dWho += np.outer(do, H[t+1])
    dh = Who.T @ do + dh_next                    # eq. (18): local + from the future
    print(f"t={t+1}: dL/do = {do}  dL/dh = {dh}")
    da = dh * (1 - H[t+1]**2)                    # through tanh
    dWhh += np.outer(da, H[t]); dWhx += np.outer(da, X[t]); dh_next = Whh.T @ da
print("dL/dWho =\n", dWho, "\ndL/dWhh =\n", dWhh, "\ndL/dWhx =\n", dWhx)
# finite-difference check of one entry
eps = 1e-6; W2 = Whh.copy(); W2[0, 1] += eps; h_ = np.zeros(2); l2 = 0
for x, y in zip(X, Y): h_ = np.tanh(W2 @ h_ + Whx @ x); l2 -= np.log(sm(Who @ h_) @ y)
print(f"finite-difference dL/dWhh[0,1] = {(l2 - loss)/eps:.4f} (BPTT {dWhh[0,1]:.4f})")

# --- Vanishing gradients ---
for k in (5, 10, 20): print(f"(0.8 x 0.5)^{k} = {0.4**k:.2e}")

code.title: 2-layer RNN, a GRU step and an LSTM step
code.explain: Recomputes the stacked-RNN example, the full GRU example (matching the worked examples) and an illustrative LSTM step.
mistakes: Mixing up the update-gate convention (z·h_old + (1 − z)·h̃ vs the reverse).
code.notes: PyTorch's GRU uses h_t = (1 − z)·n + z·h_{t−1}, the same convention as the equation (34).
code.code:
# Stacked RNN example, the session's GRU step, and an LSTM step (NumPy)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
sg = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# --- 2-layer RNN ---
Wx1 = np.array([[0.5, 0.2], [0.3, 0.4]]); Wh1 = np.array([[0.4, 0.2], [0.1, 0.3]])
Wx2 = np.array([[0.3, 0.5], [0.4, 0.2]]); Wh2 = np.array([[0.3, 0.1], [0.2, 0.4]])
h1 = h2 = np.zeros(2)
for t, x in enumerate([np.array([1., 0.]), np.array([0., 1.])], 1):
    h1 = np.tanh(Wh1 @ h1 + Wx1 @ x); h2 = np.tanh(Wh2 @ h2 + Wx2 @ h1)
    print(f"deep RNN t={t}: layer1 h = {h1}  layer2 h = {h2}")

# --- GRU step, convention h_t = z*h_prev + (1-z)*h_cand (eq. 34) ---
Wr = np.array([[0.3, 0.2], [0.1, 0.4]]); Ur = np.array([[0.5, 0.1], [0.2, 0.3]])
Wz = np.array([[0.4, 0.3], [0.2, 0.5]]); Uz = np.array([[0.3, 0.2], [0.1, 0.4]])
Wh = np.array([[0.5, 0.3], [0.2, 0.4]]); Uh = np.array([[0.4, 0.2], [0.1, 0.3]])
x = np.array([1.0, 0.5]); hp = np.array([0.6, 0.4])
r = sg(Wr @ x + Ur @ hp); z = sg(Wz @ x + Uz @ hp); hc = np.tanh(Wh @ x + Uh @ (r * hp)); h = z * hp + (1 - z) * hc
print(f"GRU: r = {r}  z = {z}  r*h_prev = {r*hp}  h_cand = {hc}  h = {h}")
print(f"GRU: share of old state = {z}, of candidate = {1-z}")

# --- LSTM step (illustrative weights: a commonly quoted version gives equations but no numeric LSTM example) ---
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); dh = 2
W = {g: rng.normal(0, 0.5, (dh, 2)) for g in "fioc"}; U = {g: rng.normal(0, 0.5, (dh, dh)) for g in "fioc"}
b = {"f": np.ones(dh), "i": np.zeros(dh), "o": np.zeros(dh), "c": np.zeros(dh)}   # forget bias 1: start by remembering
c = np.array([0.5, -0.3]); h = np.array([0.6, 0.4])
f = sg(W["f"] @ x + U["f"] @ h + b["f"]); i = sg(W["i"] @ x + U["i"] @ h + b["i"]); o = sg(W["o"] @ x + U["o"] @ h + b["o"])
cc = np.tanh(W["c"] @ x + U["c"] @ h + b["c"]); c_new = f * c + i * cc; h_new = o * np.tanh(c_new)
print(f"LSTM: f = {f}  i = {i}  o = {o}  c_cand = {cc}")
print(f"LSTM: c = f*c_prev + i*c_cand = {c_new}  h = o*tanh(c) = {h_new}  dc_t/dc_prev (gates fixed) = f = {f}")

# --- Gradient survival over 50 steps: vanilla factor vs LSTM forget gate ---
for name, fac in [("vanilla, |phi'|*||W||=0.4", 0.4), ("LSTM, f=0.95", 0.95), ("LSTM, f=0.99", 0.99)]:
    print(f"{name}: gradient after 50 steps x {fac**50:.2e}")
